system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}
user:
CONCEPT: Partial recursive function
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Definition by closure of zero, successor, and projections under composition, primitive recursion, and unbounded minimization, handling of undefined values, the distinction between partial recursive, general (total) recursive, and regular functions. Excludes primitive recursive details and the normal form theorem.

ATOMS:
- CS-COMP-C07-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: The set of partial recursive functions is the smallest set of partial functions from the natural numbers to the natural numbers (of various arities) that contains zero, successor, and the projection functions and is closed under composition, primitive recursion, and unbounded search.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0069-s01] Definition 2.26. The set of partial recursive functions is the smallest set of partial functions from the natural numbers to the natural numbers (of various arities) containing zero, successor, and projections, and closed under composition, primitive recursion, and unbounded search.
- CS-COMP-C07-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: For a partial function $f(x,\vec{z})$ on the natural numbers, the unbounded search $\mu x\, f(x,\vec{z})$ is defined to be the least $x$ such that $f(0,\vec{z}), f(1,\vec{z}), \ldots, f(x,\vec{z})$ are all defined and $f(x,\vec{z})=0$, if such an $x$ exists, and is undefined otherwise.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0068-s05] If f (x, ⃗z) is any partial function on the natural numbers, define 𝜇x f (x, ⃗z) to be
    [CS-COMP-p0068-s06] the least x such that f (0, ⃗z), f (1, ⃗z),. . . , f (x, ⃗z) are all defined, and f (x, ⃗z) = 0, if such an x exists
    [CS-COMP-p0068-s07] with the understanding that 𝜇x f (x, ⃗z) is undefined otherwise.
- CS-COMP-C07-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: The set of recursive functions (also called total recursive functions) is the set of those partial recursive functions that are total, that is, defined for every argument.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0069-s03] Definition 2.27. The set of recursive functions is the set of partial recursive functions that are total.
- CS-COMP-C07-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: When $h$ and $g_0, \ldots, g_k$ are partial functions, the composition $h(g_0(\vec{x}), \ldots, g_k(\vec{x}))$ is defined if and only if each $g_i$ is defined at $\vec{x}$ and $h$ is defined at $g_0(\vec{x}), \ldots, g_k(\vec{x})$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0068-s01] convention that if h and g0, . . . , gk all are partial functions, then
    [CS-COMP-p0068-s02] is defined if and only if each gi is defined at ⃗x, and h is defined at g0(⃗x), . . . , gk (⃗x).
- CS-COMP-C07-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Computing $\mu x\, f(x,\vec{z})$ amounts to computing $f(0,\vec{z}), f(1,\vec{z}), f(2,\vec{z}), \ldots$ until a value of 0 is returned, and if any of the intermediate computations does not halt, then the computation of $\mu x\, f(x,\vec{z})$ does not halt either.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0068-s12] The procedure for computing 𝜇x f (x, ⃗z) will amount to this: compute f (0, ⃗z), f (1, ⃗z), f (2, ⃗z) until a value of 0 is returned.
    [CS-COMP-p0068-s13] If any of the intermediate computations do not halt, however, neither does the computation of 𝜇x f (x, ⃗z).
- CS-COMP-C07-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: The definitions of composition and primitive recursion for partial functions are the same as for total functions except that "$=$" is replaced by "$\simeq$", where $f(x) \simeq g(x)$ means that either $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are both undefined, or they are both defined and equal.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0067-s16] We will use f (x) ≃g (x) to mean that either f (x) and g (x) are both undefined, or they are both defined and equal.
    [CS-COMP-p0068-s03] With this understanding, the definitions of composition and primitive recursion for partial functions is just as above, except that we have to replace “=” by “≃”.
- CS-COMP-C07-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: A total function $f(x,\vec{z})$ is regular if for every sequence of natural numbers $\vec{z}$ there is an $x$ such that $f(x,\vec{z}) = 0$, and the regular functions are exactly those to which unbounded search can be applied and still yield a total function.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0072-s03] Say a total function f (x, ⃗z) is regular if for every sequence of natural numbers ⃗z, there is an x such that f (x, ⃗z) = 0.
    [CS-COMP-p0072-s04] In other words, the regular functions are exactly those functions to which one can apply unbounded search, and end up with a total function.
- CS-COMP-C07-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Although the definition of general recursive functions (which restricts unbounded search to regular functions) differs from the definition of recursive functions (total partial recursive functions, which may use partial recursive functions along the way), the set of general recursive functions and the set of recursive functions are one and the same.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0072-s08] The difference between Definition 2.30 and Definition 2.27 is that in the latter one is allowed to use partial recursive functions along the way; the only requirement is that the function you end up with at the end is total.
    [CS-COMP-p0072-s10] But, fortunately, the difference is illusory; though the definitions are different, the set of general recursive functions and the set of recursive functions are one and the same.
- CS-COMP-C07-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: The set of general recursive functions, defined as the smallest set of functions containing zero, successor, and projections and closed under composition, primitive recursion, and unbounded search applied only to regular functions, is the same set as the set of recursive functions (the total partial recursive functions), even though the general recursive definition looks less general because the latter definition allows partial recursive functions to be used along the way.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0072-s06] Definition 2.30. The set of general recursive functions is the smallest set of functions from the natural numbers to the natural numbers (of various arities) containing zero, successor, and projections, and closed under composition, primitive recursion, and unbounded search applied to regular functions.
